Greywater Recycling & Treatment

Distinguish greywater from blackwater, design treatment systems (settling, sand filtration, reed beds), assess water quality, select appropriate soaps, plan system maintenance, and integrate greywater for irrigation and toilet flushing.

Overview

Greywater is wastewater from sinks, showers, washing machines, and laundry—containing soap, oils, food particles. It is distinct from blackwater (human waste from toilets), which requires treatment before reuse. Greywater, when treated simply, can irrigate gardens, flush toilets, or recharge groundwater, reducing freshwater demand by 30–50%.

Untreated greywater contaminates soils and groundwater. Treatment methods range from simple (settling tanks) to complex (constructed wetlands, sand filters). Proper design and maintenance determine success.

Greywater vs. Blackwater Classification

Greywater sources:

  • Sink water (kitchen, bathroom).
  • Shower/bath water.
  • Washing machine discharge.
  • Laundry water.

Blackwater sources:

  • Toilet discharge.
  • Septic tank effluent (partially treated blackwater).

Distinction matters: Greywater contains food particles, soap, oils; blackwater contains pathogens and human feces. Greywater requires simple treatment (settling, filtration); blackwater requires advanced treatment (biological breakdown, chemical disinfection) or composting toilets.

Mixed water: If greywater and blackwater combine, treat as blackwater (more stringent).

Greywater Quality Parameters

Parameter Kitchen Sink Bathroom Sink Shower Washing Machine
Suspended solids High (food) Low–medium Low High (lint)
Oil/grease Very high Medium Low–medium Low
Organic matter (BOD) Very high Medium Low–medium Medium
Nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) High (food waste) Medium Low Medium
Typical reuse Not direct irrigation; settle first Direct irrigation OK Direct irrigation OK Settle before reuse

BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand): Measure of organic contamination.

Clean water: <2 mg/L
Greywater (average): 100–300 mg/L
Acceptable for irrigation after treatment: <50 mg/L

Treatment System Design

Treatment removes solids and organic matter, making water suitable for irrigation or toilet reuse.

Settling Tank (Simplest)

Gravity separates solids (sink to bottom) from liquid (clear on top). Solids (sludge) accumulate; liquid is drawn off for irrigation or secondary treatment.

Design:

Tank volume = 1–2 days worth of greywater flow

Example: Household of 4 people
Daily greywater: 80 gallons (200 L)
Tank size: 160–320 gallons (2–3 days retention)

Typical tank: 500-gallon tank allows 48-hour settling (fine for routine use)

Retention time: 24–48 hours (longer settles more solids; reduces turbidity).

Construction:

- Rectangular or cylindrical tank.
- Inlet: 6–12 inches below surface (prevents floating debris from entering outlet).
- Outlet: 6–12 inches below surface (draws off clearer water; avoids bottom sludge).
- Overflow: Pipe directed to main sewer (if tank fills beyond capacity).
- Access: Removable lid for cleanout.
- Sludge outlet: Valve on tank bottom for periodic sludge removal.

Maintenance:

  • Pump/remove sludge every 3–6 months (accumulates ~0.5 gallons per person per month).
  • Check inlet/outlet pipes (blockages reduce flow).
  • Clean tank interior annually (algae growth if exposed to light).

Limitations:

  • Only removes solids; oils and dissolved organics remain.
  • Outlet water still turbid if solids are colloidal (suspended, won't settle).
  • Odor if anaerobic (oxygen-depleted).

Sand Filtration

Sand acts as a physical and biological filter. Water trickles through sand; particles are trapped; bacteria degrade organics.

Design (sand filter for greywater):

Depth: 24–36 inches of sand (0.5–1 meter)
Sand grain size: Medium to coarse (0.5–2 mm diameter)
Support layer: 6–12 inches gravel beneath sand (prevents sand loss)
Drainage layer: Perforated pipe in gravel (collects filtered water)

Bed size: 1 square foot per 5 gallons per day
Example: 100 gallons/day greywater → 20 square feet bed

Operation:

  1. Settle greywater: Pre-treatment in settling tank (removes large solids).
  2. Distribute: Water distributed evenly across sand surface (perforated manifold or drip line).
  3. Infiltrate: Water percolates downward through sand.
  4. Drainage: Filtered water exits through drainage layer; collected in underdrain pipe.

Performance:

  • Turbidity reduction: 90%+ (water clarity improves dramatically).
  • BOD reduction: 50–80% (biological activity in sand breaks down organics).
  • Pathogen reduction: 90%+ (physical filtration + biological decay).
  • Effectiveness: Requires 48+ hours contact time (slow); not suitable for high-flow systems.

Constructed Wetlands (Reed Beds)

Wetland plants and soil biofilm treat water biologically; also removes nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus).

Design:

Configuration: Horizontal flow (water moves horizontally through planted bed) or vertical flow (water trickles downward)

Dimensions (per 10 gallons/day flow):
- Area: 1–2 square feet
- Depth: 12–24 inches

Substrate (growing medium):
- Layer 1 (bottom): 3–6 inches gravel (drainage)
- Layer 2: 8–12 inches sand/soil mix
- Layer 3 (top): 2–6 inches topsoil (planting)

Plants: Cattails, reeds, rushes (remove nutrients, provide habitat for microbes)

Operation:

  1. Pre-treat: Settle greywater to remove large solids.
  2. Distribute: Feed into inlet of reed bed at subsurface level.
  3. Plant action: Plants uptake nitrogen/phosphorus; roots host biofilm bacteria.
  4. Drainage: Water exits through outlet pipe; ready for reuse or discharge.

Performance:

  • BOD reduction: 80–95%.
  • Nitrogen removal: 60–80% (plants + denitrification).
  • Phosphorus removal: 50–70% (soil absorption + plant uptake).
  • Pathogen reduction: 90%+.
  • Aesthetic: Green, planted bed (visually appealing vs. mechanical systems).

Maintenance:

  • Vegetation: Trim annually (prevents overgrowth); replant as needed.
  • Substrate: Replace every 10+ years (accumulates sludge over time).
  • Inspection: Monitor water level (should remain subsurface); check outlet (blockages).

Comparison Table

System Cost Space Maintenance Performance Aesthetics
Settling tank $500–1,500 Small (2–3 sq ft footprint) Moderate (sludge removal) Low (solids only) Industrial
Sand filter $1,500–3,000 Medium (20 sq ft typical) Moderate (clogging, replacement) Moderate–high Utilitarian
Reed bed $2,000–4,000 Large (30+ sq ft) Low (vegetation management) High Natural, attractive

Water Quality Assessment

Before reuse, test treated greywater to ensure safety.

Simple Tests (no equipment)

Visual:

Color: Clear = good; cloudy = suspended solids (requires further treatment)
Odor: Neutral = good; sour/musty = organic decomposition (incomplete treatment)

Settling test:

Fill clear jar with treated water; observe for 24 hours.
If solids settle to bottom, water is suitable for irrigation (gravity-separated).
If cloudiness remains, requires sand filtration.

Laboratory Tests (if available)

Parameter Safe Level for Irrigation Test Method
BOD <50 mg/L Biochemical oxygen demand (microbial test, 5 days)
Turbidity <5 NTU Turbidity meter (measures light transmission)
Nitrogen <50 mg/L N Chemical test (Kjeldahl or equivalent)
Phosphorus <10 mg/L P Chemical test (colorimetric method)
Pathogens <100 CFU/100 mL Microbial culture (indicator organisms)

Simple testing substitutes:

If testing unavailable, assume 50% reduction in each treatment stage:
Settling tank: 50% BOD reduction
Sand filter: Additional 70% reduction (cumulative 85% from raw greywater)
Reed bed: Additional 90% reduction (cumulative 95%+)

Conservative approach: Use treated greywater only for non-food crops or toilet flushing (does not require potable quality).

Soap and Detergent Selection

Soaps affect greywater quality and treatment efficacy. Some are compatible with plant irrigation; others accumulate and damage soil.

Soap Types and Compatibility

Type Source Biodegradability Plant Effects Recommendation
Bar soap (tallow/palm oil) Rendered animal fat or plant oil High (biodegrades in 5–7 days) Minimal (plants tolerate) Good for greywater systems
Detergent (synthetic) Petroleum-based surfactants Variable (some resist breakdown) Sodium/phosphate buildup Limit or avoid
Castile soap (plant oil) Coconut, olive, or other oil High Minimal Excellent
Gray-water specific soap Biodegradable, no additives Very high Minimal Ideal
Typical shampoo/body wash Synthetic with fragrances, additives Variable Possible accumulation Avoid if possible

Soil buildup risk:

Synthetic detergents contain sodium salts and phosphates.
Over time, they accumulate in soil, increasing pH and salinity.
Accumulated sodium clogs soil pores, reducing water infiltration.
Phosphate buildup causes algal blooms in surface waters if greywater drains to them.

Solution: Use plant-based soaps; avoid high-phosphate laundry detergents.
Test soil every 2 years (salinity, pH, phosphorus levels).

Greywater-Safe Practices

Choose soaps with:

  • No synthetic dyes or fragrances (persist in soil).
  • No added sodium (sodium accumulates; use potassium-based soaps if labeled).
  • Biodegradable surfactants (break down quickly).

Avoid soaps with:

  • Boron (toxic to plants in high concentrations).
  • Bleach or oxidizing agents (kill soil microbes).
  • Petroleum distillates or solvents (persist in soil).

Practical approach:

Make soap at home (rendered animal fat or vegetable oil + lye); or purchase commercial greywater-safe soaps. Cost ~$2–5 per pound (similar to conventional soap).

System Maintenance and Troubleshooting

Monthly tasks:

  • Check inlet/outlet flows (blockages reduce efficiency).
  • Observe water quality (settling tank: solids accumulation; sand filter: water clarity).
  • Inspect vegetation (reed beds: wilting or disease).
  • Monitor odors (sign of anaerobic breakdown or stagnation).

Quarterly tasks:

  • Remove sludge from settling tank (if accumulated >6 inches).
  • Check drainage pipes for blockages (root intrusion, sediment).
  • Vegetation maintenance (reed beds: trim dead plants).

Annual tasks:

  • Flushing settling tank (remove accumulated sludge).
  • Sand filter surface cleaning (remove clogged layer).
  • Soil testing (reed beds: salinity, pH, phosphorus).
  • System performance evaluation (compare treated water quality to baseline).

Troubleshooting:

Problem Cause Solution
Slow drainage Clogged inlet/outlet pipes Flush with clean water; unclog with snake/pressure washer
Foul odor Anaerobic conditions (low oxygen) Aerate (add oxygen); reduce organic input; increase flow
Cloudy treated water Inadequate settling/filtration Extend retention time; add sand layer; increase filter depth
Algae growth (in open tank) Light exposure + nutrients Cover tank; reduce nutrient input (food waste pre-screening)
Plant wilting (reed beds) Poor drainage or waterlogging Check outlet; adjust water level
Mosquito breeding Standing water Drain or treat standing water; maintain water circulation

Greywater Reuse Applications

Potential uses (descending order of safety):

  1. Irrigation (non-food crops): Ornamental plants, trees, shrubs. Lowest safety concern (no direct human contact).
  2. Toilet flushing: Multiple flushes/day; water never enters human system.
  3. Cleaning/washing: Hard surfaces (not food-contact surfaces).
  4. Food crop irrigation: Only after advanced treatment (nearly potable quality). Requires careful management.

Design example (household 4 people, 80 gallons/day greywater):

System: Settling tank → Sand filter → Reuse tank.

Settling tank (240 gallons): 3-day retention
Accumulation: 6 gallons sludge per month (remove quarterly)

Sand filter bed (25 sq feet): 1.5 days contact time
Output: ~70 gallons/day treated water

Reuse applications:
- Garden irrigation: 30–40 gallons (perennials, trees)
- Toilet flushing (dual-flush): 20–30 gallons (4 people × 4–6 flushes/day)
- Surplus: 10–15 gallons discharged or stored for dry-season use

Toilet flushing system:

  • Separate greywater tank (300–500 gallons) from toilet supply.
  • Float valve maintains level (refills from greywater discharge; falls back to main water if greywater insufficient).
  • Cost: $500–1,500 (tank, plumbing, valve).
  • Water savings: 20–30 gallons/day (30–40% reduction for typical household).

Design Example: 4-Person Household Greywater System

Household: 4 people; daily water use 200 gallons (50 gallons per person).

Greywater sources:

  • Shower: 50 gallons.
  • Sink (kitchen/bath): 30 gallons.
  • Laundry: 40 gallons.
  • Total: 120 gallons/day greywater.

Blackwater (excluded from system): 40 gallons toilet discharge/day (treated separately with composting toilet or septic system).

Goal: Reuse greywater for toilet flushing and landscape irrigation; reduce freshwater demand by 50%.

System design:

Component Specification Cost
Settling tank 300-gallon (36-hour retention) $800
Sand filter bed 25 sq feet (1.5-foot depth) $1,200
Reuse tank (toilet flushing) 300-gallon $600
Plumbing (valves, pipes, fittings) PVC, dual-flush toilet valve $400
Total system cost - $3,000

Performance:

Daily greywater: 120 gallons
Treatment: Settling (50% improvement) + Sand filter (70% additional)
Treated water: ~100–110 gallons suitable for reuse

Daily uses:
- Toilet flushing: 20–25 gallons (needs)
- Garden irrigation: 60–70 gallons (nonpotable OK)
- Excess/storage: 10–20 gallons

Seasonal variation:
- Summer (garden demand high): All treated water used
- Winter (garden dormant): Toilet flushing needs 20–25 gallons; surplus 80–85 gallons (discharged or stored)

Annual water savings: 120 gallons/day × 365 = 43,800 gallons (~$200–300 in water/sewer costs, depending on region)

Payback period: 10–15 years (if accounting for water savings); faster if drought restrictions increase water costs.
